title: Strings and String Methods
summary: Inspect, search, slice, transform, pad, split, and join text with JavaScript's everyday string methods.
intro: Almost every program handles text: names, emails, codes, and sentences. JavaScript strings come with a toolbox of methods for reading, searching, cutting, and rebuilding them, and none of them ever change the original string.

steps.title: Length, indexes, and immutability
steps.body:
A string is a sequence of characters. `str.length` counts them, and `str[i]` reads one by its zero-based index, just like an array. For the last character use `str.at(-1)`: negative numbers count from the end. Plain `str[-1]` gives `undefined`, and so does any index past the end. One gotcha: most emoji count as 2 toward `length`, because JavaScript stores them as two UTF-16 units. The next lesson shows how to count them as one.

```javascript
const word = "code";
console.log(word.length); // 4
console.log(word[0]);     // c
console.log(word.at(-1)); // e
```

**Strings are immutable.** You cannot change a character in place. In this script `word[0] = "C"` is silently ignored (strict-mode code would throw a TypeError). Every string method you meet in this lesson returns a *new* string and leaves the original alone.

Compare strings with `===` for equality and `<` or `>` for order. Order goes by character code, character by character, and every uppercase letter comes before every lowercase one. So `"Zebra" < "apple"` is true, and `"10" < "9"` is true too, because `"1"` comes before `"9"`.

example.title: Inspecting JavaScript
example.prompt: Read the length and a few characters of a word, try to change it, and compare some strings.
example.output:
Length: 10
First: J
Last: t
Index 4: S
After word[0] = "j": JavaScript
Same word: true
"apple" < "banana": true
"Zebra" < "apple": true
example.explanation: `word.length` is 10, `word[0]` is `J`, and `word.at(-1)` is `t`. Index 4 is the capital `S`. The assignment `word[0] = "j"` does nothing, so the word prints unchanged. `"apple" < "banana"` is true because `a` comes before `b`. `"Zebra" < "apple"` is also true because uppercase `Z` has a smaller character code than lowercase `a`.

practice.title: Inspecting a username
practice.prompt:
Inspect a username, try to change it, and compare two words.

1. Print `Length: ` followed by `username.length`.
2. Print `First: ` and `Last: ` lines using `username[0]` and `username.at(-1)`.
3. Print `Index 3: ` followed by `username[3]`.
4. Assign `"A"` to `username[0]`, then print `After username[0] = "A": ` followed by the username.
5. Print `"cat" < "Cat": ` followed by the result of that comparison.

Expected output:

```text
Length: 12
First: a
Last: e
Index 3: _
After username[0] = "A": ada_lovelace
"cat" < "Cat": false
```

tests.output:
Length: 12
First: a
Last: e
Index 3: _
After username[0] = "A": ada_lovelace
"cat" < "Cat": false

hints: Indexes start at 0, so `username[3]` is the fourth character.
The assignment to `username[0]` is ignored, so the username prints exactly as it started.
Lowercase letters have larger character codes than uppercase ones, so `"cat" < "Cat"` is false.

steps.title: Case, trimming, and searching
steps.body:
Real text is messy, so clean it before you check it. `toUpperCase()` and `toLowerCase()` change the case. `trim()` removes whitespace from both ends, while `trimStart()` and `trimEnd()` remove it from one end only. Methods chain because each returns a new string:

```javascript
console.log("  Hello ".trim().toLowerCase()); // hello
```

To search, use these:

- `includes(sub)` is true when `sub` appears anywhere.
- `startsWith(prefix)` and `endsWith(suffix)` check the ends.
- `indexOf(sub)` gives the index of the first match, `lastIndexOf(sub)` the last one.

Both index methods return `-1` when there is no match, so test with `!== -1`, never with truthiness: a match at index 0 is falsy and a miss (`-1`) is truthy. Every search is case-sensitive, so `"Hello".includes("hello")` is false. That is why you normalize the case first.

example.title: Cleaning an email
example.prompt: Clean up a messy email address, then search it.
example.output:
[Ada@Example.COM ]
[  Ada@Example.COM]
Clean: ada@example.com
Has @: true
Starts with ada: true
Ends with .com: true
@ at index: 3
# at index: -1
Last . at index: 11
Upper: ADA@EXAMPLE.COM
example.explanation: The brackets show which spaces `trimStart()` and `trimEnd()` removed. `trim().toLowerCase()` produces `ada@example.com` in one chain, and `rawEmail` itself never changes. The searches run on the clean copy, so case and stray spaces cannot break them. The `@` sits at index 3, and `#` is missing, so `indexOf` returns -1. `lastIndexOf` finds the dot before `com` at index 11.

practice.title: Cleaning a product code
practice.prompt:
Clean up a messy product code, then search it.

1. Print `rawCode.trimStart()` and then `rawCode.trimEnd()`, each wrapped in square brackets.
2. Trim `rawCode` and make it uppercase, storing the result in `code`.
3. Print `Clean: ` followed by `code`.
4. Print `Starts with SKU: `, `Ends with RED: `, and `Has BLUE: ` lines with `startsWith`, `endsWith`, and `includes`.
5. Print `First dash: ` and `Last dash: ` lines with `indexOf("-")` and `lastIndexOf("-")`.

Expected output:

```text
[sku-4471-blue  ]
[  sku-4471-blue]
Clean: SKU-4471-BLUE
Starts with SKU: true
Ends with RED: false
Has BLUE: true
First dash: 3
Last dash: 8
```

tests.output:
[sku-4471-blue  ]
[  sku-4471-blue]
Clean: SKU-4471-BLUE
Starts with SKU: true
Ends with RED: false
Has BLUE: true
First dash: 3
Last dash: 8

hints: Trim first, then change the case. Each method returns a new string, so you can chain the two calls.
Search `code`, not `rawCode`. The raw text is still lowercase with spaces around it.
`lastIndexOf` searches from the end, so it finds the second dash.

steps.title: Slicing, replacing, and padding
steps.body:
`slice(start, end)` copies the characters from `start` up to, but not including, `end`. Leave out `end` to go to the finish. Negative indexes count from the end, so `slice(-4)` is the last four characters. `substring(start, end)` does the same for non-negative indexes, but it treats a negative index as 0 and swaps its arguments when `start` is bigger than `end`, so prefer `slice`.

```javascript
const id = "AB-12345";
console.log(id.slice(0, 2));  // AB
console.log(id.slice(-3));    // 345
console.log(id.substring(3)); // 12345
```

`replace(old, new)` swaps **only the first match** when `old` is a string. Use `replaceAll(old, new)` to change every match. This surprises people coming from other languages.

`repeat(n)` repeats a string `n` times. `padStart(width, char)` and `padEnd(width, char)` add `char` until the string is `width` long, which lines up columns in text output. Leave out `char` to pad with spaces. A string already at or past the width comes back unchanged.

example.title: Card and receipt
example.prompt: Mask a card number, fix up a date, and print two aligned receipt rows.
example.output:
Masked: ************4444
First four: 4111
Digits 5-8: 2222
replace: 2024/01-15
replaceAll: 2024/01/15
Coffee......3.50
Bagel......12.25
example.explanation: `"*".repeat(12)` makes twelve stars, and `card.slice(-4)` keeps the last four digits. `substring(0, 4)` and `slice(4, 8)` copy ranges with the end index left out. `replace` changes only the first dash, while `replaceAll` changes both. On the receipt, `padEnd(10, ".")` widens each name to 10 characters and `padStart(6, ".")` pushes each price to the right of a 6-character column, so both rows are 16 characters and the prices line up.

practice.title: Phone and menu
practice.prompt:
Mask a phone number, fix up a sentence, and print one aligned menu row.

1. Print `Masked: ` followed by six `*` characters (use `repeat`) and the last four digits of `phone` (use `slice`).
2. Print `Area code: ` followed by the first three digits with `substring`.
3. Print `replace: ` followed by `sentence` with the first `cat` changed to `dog`.
4. Print `replaceAll: ` followed by `sentence` with every `cat` changed to `dog`.
5. Print `Tea` padded on the right with `.` to 10 characters, followed directly by `2.75` padded on the left with `.` to 6 characters.

Expected output:

```text
Masked: ******4567
Area code: 555
replace: the dog saw another cat
replaceAll: the dog saw another dog
Tea.........2.75
```

tests.output:
Masked: ******4567
Area code: 555
replace: the dog saw another cat
replaceAll: the dog saw another dog
Tea.........2.75

hints: `phone.length - 4` is 6, which is how many stars you need.
`replace` with a string changes only the first match. `replaceAll` changes them all.
Use `padEnd(10, ".")` on the name and `padStart(6, ".")` on the price, then put the two results side by side.

steps.title: split and join
steps.body:
`split(separator)` cuts a string at every separator and returns an array of the pieces. `join(separator)` does the reverse: it glues an array's items into one string with the separator between them.

```javascript
const parts = "a,b,c".split(",");
console.log(parts);             // [ 'a', 'b', 'c' ]
console.log(parts.join(" + ")); // a + b + c
console.log("hi".split(""));    // [ 'h', 'i' ]
```

`split("")` gives one item per character, which makes array methods available for text. To reverse a string, split it, reverse the array, and join: `str.split("").reverse().join("")`. This is fine for plain letters, but `split("")` cuts an emoji into two broken halves. The next lesson shows a safer way.

The pieces are always strings. Convert them with `Number()` before you do math, or `+` will glue text: `0 + "10"` is `"010"`. If the separator never appears, you get an array with the whole string as its only item. Two separators in a row leave an empty string between them: `"a,,b".split(",")` is `["a", "", "b"]`, and `Number("")` is 0, not NaN.

example.title: Colors and numbers
example.prompt: Split a list of colors, rebuild it in a few ways, and add up numbers stored in a string.
example.output:
Count: 3
Colors: red | green | blue
Letters: b-l-u-e
Reversed: eulb
Sum: 60
example.explanation: Splitting on `","` gives three color strings, and `join(" | ")` puts them back together with a new separator. `split("")` breaks `blue` into letters, so joining with `-` spaces them out, and `reverse()` before the join spells the word backwards. The numbers arrive as the strings `"10"`, `"20"`, and `"30"`, so `Number(part)` converts each one before it is added.

practice.title: Words and numbers
practice.prompt:
Split a sentence into words, rebuild it in a few ways, and multiply numbers stored in a string.

1. Split `sentence` on spaces into `words`, then print `Count: ` followed by the number of words.
2. Print `Words: ` followed by the words joined with `-`.
3. Take the last word and print `Letters: ` followed by its letters joined with `.`.
4. Print `Reversed: ` followed by the last word spelled backwards.
5. Split `numbers` on `:`, multiply the parts as numbers starting from 1, and print `Product: ` followed by the result.

Expected output:

```text
Count: 4
Words: the-quick-brown-fox
Letters: f.o.x
Reversed: xof
Product: 120
```

tests.output:
Count: 4
Words: the-quick-brown-fox
Letters: f.o.x
Reversed: xof
Product: 120

hints: To spell a word backwards, split it into letters, reverse the array, and join with an empty string.
Start `product` at 1, not 0, and convert each part with `Number()` before you multiply.

recap:
- `str.length` counts characters (most emoji count as 2), `str[i]` reads one, and `str.at(-1)` reads the last.
- Strings are immutable: `str[0] = "x"` does nothing, and every method returns a new string.
- `===` checks for an exact match, and `<` compares by character code, so uppercase sorts before lowercase.
- `toUpperCase()`, `toLowerCase()`, `trim()`, `trimStart()`, and `trimEnd()` clean text.
- `includes`, `startsWith`, and `endsWith` return true or false. `indexOf` and `lastIndexOf` return an index or -1.
- `slice(start, end)` copies a range, with negative indexes counting from the end. `substring` is similar but treats negative indexes as 0.
- `replace` changes only the first match, `replaceAll` changes every match.
- `repeat`, `padStart`, and `padEnd` build and align text, padding with spaces by default.
- `split` turns a string into an array of strings, `join` turns an array back into a string, and `Number()` converts the pieces for math.
